title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
description: Count, for each index, how many smaller values appear to its right, using an index-tracking modified merge sort.

sections.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

content.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given an integer array nums, return an array counts where counts[i] is the number of elements to the RIGHT of index i that are smaller than nums[i].

blocks.caption: A modified merge sort, tracking original indices, counts smaller-to-the-right values during the merge step.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums[] (can contain negatives and duplicates)"],["Output","counts[] (same length), counts[i] = number of j > i with nums[j] < nums[i]"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

This is the index-tracking sibling of Reverse Pairs: instead of counting cross-half pairs satisfying a value condition, it counts, for EACH left element, how many right-half elements are smaller, attributing that count back to the ORIGINAL index. Merge sort naturally computes this during the merge step, since both halves are sorted by value at that point.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: Whenever "count smaller/larger elements after this position" is asked across a WHOLE array, modified merge sort tracking indices (not just values) is the standard technique, closely related to counting inversions.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture two lines of runners merging into one finish line, sorted by speed. As a runner from the LEFT line steps into the merged line, count how many faster (smaller value) right-line runners have ALREADY stepped in ahead of them; that count is exactly how many right-half elements are smaller than this left element.

blocks.caption: Counting right-line runners already merged in gives the smaller-to-the-right count directly.

items: Sort by INDEX-carrying values, not raw values, so each count can be attributed back to the correct original position.
During merge, whenever a left element is placed into the merged result, add the number of right elements already placed (since they are smaller and originally to its right).
Recursing bottom-up means the count for each index accumulates correctly across every level of the merge sort.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
nums = [5,2,6,1]. Track indices through the merge sort.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Merge step","Left indices (values)","Right indices (values)","Counts after this step"],"rows":[["1","idx 0 (5)","idx 1 (2)","2 < 5, counts[0] += 1 -> [1,0,0,0]"],["2","idx 2 (6)","idx 3 (1)","1 < 6, counts[2] += 1 -> [1,0,1,0]"],["3 (top)","idx 1, idx 0 (2, 5)","idx 3, idx 2 (1, 6)","1 < 2 first (rightCount=1); then 6 is not < 2, so counts[1] += 1; then 6 is not < 5, so counts[0] += 1 -> final [2,1,1,0]"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Accumulating counts across all merge steps gives [2,1,1,0], matching the expected output: 5 has 2 smaller values to its right (2 and 1), 2 has 1 (just 1), 6 has 1 (just 1), and 1 has 0.
5. How Should We Think?
A direct approach checks every pair (i, j) with j > i directly, counting smaller values. This is correct but quadratic.

Modified merge sort, tracking indices through the recursion, lets the counting happen naturally during the merge step: both halves are sorted by value at that point, so a single linear merge pass can correctly attribute "how many right elements are smaller" to each left element as it is placed.
6. Brute Force Solution
Check every pair (i, j) with j > i directly for the smaller-value condition.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2)","Every pair (i, j) is checked directly"],["Space","O(n)","The counts array"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: For large n, checking every pair individually is far more work than merge sort's bulk counting during merges.
8. Optimize the Solution

Perform merge sort over an array of ORIGINAL INDICES, comparing nums[index] for ordering. During each merge, maintain a running count of right-half elements already placed; whenever a left-half element is placed (either because it is smaller, or the right half is exhausted), add that running count to counts[originalIndex].

items: Recursively merge sort indices, comparing by nums[index].
During merge, track rightCount: how many right elements have been placed so far.
Whenever a left element is placed into the merged result, add rightCount to counts at that left element's original index.

blocks.text: 9. Optimized Solution

codes.python:
def count_smaller(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    counts = [0] * n

    def merge_sort(idx_arr):
        if len(idx_arr) <= 1:
            return idx_arr

        mid = len(idx_arr) // 2
        left = merge_sort(idx_arr[:mid])
        right = merge_sort(idx_arr[mid:])

        right_count = 0
        merged = []
        li = ri = 0
        while li < len(left) and ri < len(right):
            if nums[right[ri]] < nums[left[li]]:
                right_count += 1
                merged.append(right[ri])
                ri += 1
            else:
                counts[left[li]] += right_count
                merged.append(left[li])
                li += 1
        while li < len(left):
            counts[left[li]] += right_count
            merged.append(left[li])
            li += 1
        while ri < len(right):
            merged.append(right[ri])
            ri += 1
        return merged

    merge_sort(list(range(n)))
    return counts


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(count_smaller([5, 2, 6, 1]))
    print(count_smaller([-1]))

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, all-pairs check","O(n^2)","O(n)"],["Optimized, index-tracking merge sort","O(n log n)","O(n)"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: When a per-index result (not just a global count) is needed, merge sort must track ORIGINAL INDICES through the recursion, not just values.
The counting happens naturally during the merge step, since both halves are already sorted by value at that point.
This exact technique is the direct sibling of Reverse Pairs and the classic count-inversions problem, differing only in what condition is counted and how the count is attributed.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Count of Smaller Numbers After Self is solved with a modified merge sort that tracks original indices through the recursion. During each merge, a running count of already-placed right-half elements is added to each left-half element's original index whenever it is placed, giving the correct per-index count in O(n log n) time.
